units.Nehemiah 5:1: A great outcry arose from the people and their wives against their Jewish brothers.

units.Nehemiah 5:3: Others said, “Our fields, our vineyards and our houses—we are pledging them. We must obtain grain and eat.”
units.Nehemiah 5:5: Now our flesh is like our brothers’ flesh, and our sons like their sons. Yet we are forcing our sons and daughters into slavery, and some of our daughters are being subjected. There is no power in our hands, and our fields and vineyards belong to the honored men.”
units.Nehemiah 5:6: I was deeply grieved when I heard their outcry and these words.
units.Nehemiah 5:7: My heart took counsel within me. I contended with the honored men and leaders and said to them, “You are making demands, each against his brother!” I brought a great assembly against them,
units.Nehemiah 5:8: and said to them, “We have bought our Jewish brothers who were being sold to the nations, of our own free will. And are you selling your brothers?” They fell quiet and found no answer.
units.Nehemiah 5:9: I said, “What you are doing is not good. Not so! In the fear of our God you shall depart from the reproach of the nations, our enemies.
units.Nehemiah 5:10: My brothers, my acquaintances and I have also put silver and grain at their disposal. Let us, I pray, relinquish this exaction.
units.Nehemiah 5:11: Please restore to them this very day their fields, vineyards, olive trees and houses; and from the silver, bring out for them the grain, wine and oil.”
units.Nehemiah 5:12: They said, “We will return it and ask nothing from them. We will do as you say.” I called the priests and made them swear to act according to this word.
units.Nehemiah 5:13: I shook out my wrap and said, “So may God shake out from his house and his labor every man who does not uphold this word. So shall he be shaken out and empty.” All the assembly said, “Amen,” and praised the Lord. The people carried out this word.
units.Nehemiah 5:14: From the day he appointed me to be their ruler in the land of Judah—from the twentieth year to the thirty-second year of Arthasastha, twelve years—I and my brothers did not eat their coerced provision,

final_retained_full_triples.rationale: Eliphaz says that those who sow improper things perish by the Lord's command and the breath of His anger. The letter says the Lord Jesus will kill the lawless one with the breath of His mouth. Both employ the Lord's breath as the means of overthrow, but Eliphaz's claim is not a verdict that Job is guilty, nor are his unnamed offenders identified with the letter's lawless one.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: By the Lord’s command they will perish; by the breath of His anger they will disappear.

target_units.text: And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of His mouth and bring to nothing by the manifestation of His coming.

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: Audible speech without a visible form
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: Eliphaz reports hearing a breeze and a voice while seeing no form and not recognizing the presence. Deuteronomy recalls Israel hearing words but seeing no likeness at Horeb, only a voice. The shared feature is heard speech without a visible form; Deuteronomy explicitly names the Lord as speaker, and that identity or authority is not transferred to Eliphaz's unrecognized presence.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: I stood up and did not recognize it; I looked, and there was no form before my eyes, but I heard a breeze and a voice:

target_units.text: And the Lord spoke unto you out of the midst of the fire; you heard the sound of words, but saw no likeness, only a voice.

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: Righteous benefit contrasted with the loss of the impious
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: Eliphaz's account moves from fools' ruined way of life to the righteous eating gathered goods. Proverbs explicitly says that the wealth of the impious is stored up for the righteous. Both place the righteous person's benefit beside wrongdoing's loss. The source's pronouns are not used to identify particular owners or a transaction, and the proverb does not identify Job's lost property or endorse Eliphaz's application to him.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: For the righteous will eat what they gathered, and they themselves will not be rescued from evils; may their strength be drained away.

target_units.text: A good man will inherit children’s children, but the wealth of the impious is stored up for the righteous.

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: Lament over help remaining far away
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: Job contrasts his trust with help being far from him. The psalm directly asks the Lord not to put the speaker's help far away and to attend to his support. Both express distress through the distance of help, with Job stating his experienced lack and the psalm petitioning against it; the psalm's later claim that God heard the petition is not inserted into Job's present complaint.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: Had I not trusted in Him? But help is far from me.

target_units.text: But Thou, Lord, do not put my help far away; attend to my support.

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: Petition for relief before departure from life
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: Job asks for his wrongdoing to be forgotten and his sin cleansed before he departs into the earth and is no more. The psalm asks the Lord to hear and grant relief before the speaker departs and no longer exists. Both make anticipated departure the urgent setting for a petition, while Job's request for cleansing and the psalm's request for refreshment remain distinct.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: Why hast Thou not brought about forgetfulness of my lawlessness and cleansing of my sin? But now I will depart into the earth; at daybreak I am no more.”

target_units.text: Hear my prayer, Lord, and give ear to my supplication; do not remain silent at my tears. For I am a sojourner with Thee and a temporary resident like all my fathers.
Give me relief, that I may be refreshed, before I depart and no longer exist.”

final_retained_full_triples.rationale: Job asks who grew hard against the mighty God and endured. Romans voices an imagined objection asking who has resisted God's purpose, then challenges a human being's answering back to God. Both formulate divine-human resistance as a rhetorical question. Job's complaint and Paul's reply to an objector are different arguments; neither identifies Job with Pharaoh or endorses every inference of the other speaker.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: For He is wise in understanding, mighty and great. Who grew hard against Him and endured?

target_units.text: You will then say to me, “Why, then, does He still find fault? For who has resisted His purpose?”
But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is formed say to the One who formed it, “Why didst Thou make me this way?”

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: Darkness and the land of the dead in lament
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: Job describes the land to which he expects to go as without brightness or sight of mortal life. The psalm asks whether mercy is recounted in the grave or wonders known in darkness and a forgotten land. Both laments associate death with a dark land cut off from ordinary living experience; the comparison preserves their lamenting voices and does not construct a complete account of the afterlife.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: to a land of everlasting darkness, where there is no brightness and no seeing the life of mortals.’”

target_units.text: Surely no one will recount Thy mercy in a grave and Thy truth in destruction?
Surely Thy wonders will not be known in darkness, or Thy righteousness in a forgotten land?

final_retained_full_triples.rationale: Job asks who could rebuild what God throws down or open what He shuts. In Isaiah the Lord declares that no one rescues from His hands and asks who will turn back His action. Both deny a human capacity to undo God's act. Isaiah does not supply Job's particular demolition or confinement images, and no specific prisoner or destroyed building is identified.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: If He throws down, who will build? If He shuts people in, who will open?

target_units.text: still from the beginning. No one rescues from My hands. I will act, and who will turn it back?”

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: Wind-carried leaves as an image of vulnerability
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: Job asks why God would oppose one as frail as a wind-moved leaf or grass carried by a breeze. Isaiah's communal confession depicts people falling like leaves and being carried off by wind because of their lawless deeds. The shared plant-and-wind image expresses vulnerability, while the confession's stated guilt is not imposed on Job's plea.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: Wilt Thou be wary of a leaf moved by wind, or oppose me as grass carried by a breeze?

target_units.text: We all became like unclean people; all our righteousness is like a menstruating woman’s rag. We fell away like leaves because of our lawless deeds; thus wind will carry us off.

final_retained_full_triples.rationale: Eliphaz portrays the ungodly person's life as anxiety. Isaiah pictures the unjust as wave-tossed and unable to rest, and declares no rejoicing for the ungodly. Both associate wrongdoing with unrest, but the prophetic statement does not prove Eliphaz's insinuation that Job's suffering establishes his guilt.
